title: Human-Computer Interface
description: The CCMAS course in human-computer interaction: what HCI is and how it evolved, its multidisciplinary foundations, interaction styles and accessibility, human cognition and its laws, physical ergonomics, user-centred design, GUI design principles, and system design methods and human-centred evaluation. Built from Miss P. B. Falola and Mr S. O. Fawale's INS 202 Lectures 1 to 8.

topics.title: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction
topics.summary: HCI is the multidisciplinary field concerned with the design, evaluation and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use. It differs from UI and UX, evolved from switches and command lines to GUIs, touch and natural interaction, matters for usability, productivity, safety, accessibility and business value, and has five components: user, system, interaction, task and context.
subtopics: History: from ENIAC to natural interaction
HCI as a field: SIGCHI and CHI
The five components of an interaction

topics.title: Foundations: Interaction Styles, Diversity and Accessibility
topics.summary: HCI draws on computer science, psychology, design, ergonomics, sociology and linguistics. Every interaction combines human factors (physical, cognitive, social) and computer factors (input, output, processing, dialogue style). There are six interaction styles, users are diverse, and accessibility (WCAG's POUR principles) sits within inclusive design.

topics.title: Cognition and Human Factors
topics.summary: Users perceive interfaces through vision, hearing and touch, organised by Gestalt principles. Memory moves through sensory, short-term and long-term stages, and recognition beats recall. Attention is selective or divided. Mental models, Reason's slips and mistakes, Miller's 7±2, Fitts's Law and Hick's Law explain and predict user behaviour.
subtopics: Miller's Law, Fitts's Law and Hick's Law

topics.title: Physical Ergonomics
topics.summary: Physical ergonomics fits workstations and devices to the human body. Workspace design follows ISO 9241-5 principles; keyboard, mouse and mobile design affect strain; display technology affects comfort; digital eye strain and repetitive strain injury are prevented by the 20-20-20 rule and micro-breaks; and postural variation and organisational responsibility matter most.
subtopics: Keyboards, mice and mobile thumb zones
Posture, sitting versus standing, and shared responsibility

topics.title: User-Centred Design
topics.summary: User-centred design puts users at the centre of every stage. Design thinking has five non-linear stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test. User research replaces assumptions with evidence; personas and journey maps summarise it; storyboards, wireframes and prototypes shape solutions; and iterative design refines them through feedback.
subtopics: The five stages of design thinking

topics.title: GUI Design Principles
topics.summary: Good GUI design means efficient, accurate, low-friction task completion, not visual polish alone. Nielsen's ten usability heuristics and Shneiderman's eight golden rules guide design and evaluation, supported by colour theory, typography, icon design, navigation patterns, menus and good form design.

topics.title: System Design Methods and Human-Centred Evaluation
topics.summary: System design methods structure how software is built: Waterfall is sequential, Spiral is risk-driven and iterative, Agile values iteration and collaboration, and Scrum applies Agile in fixed sprints. Human-centred evaluation tests designs with real users through formative and summative methods such as usability testing, A/B testing, heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthroughs and the System Usability Scale.
subtopics: Usability testing, A/B testing and heuristic evaluation
The System Usability Scale and other methods
